UNIONDALE GHOST TOWN

By: Latashia Naidoo | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Uniondale straddles the fragile line between myth and memory, and how communities reinvent themselves to stay alive.

Unique Selling Point:
The Uniondale Ghost has become one of South Africa’s longest-running urban legends, blending tragedy, tourism, and a touch of the supernatural.

Summary:
Tucked deep in the Little Karoo along the legendary Route 62, Uniondale looks like any other sleepy farming town - stone churches, dirt roads, and the smell of fynbos in the air. But beneath its postcard charm lies a tale that refuses to die.
In 1968, a young woman named Maria Charlotte Roux was killed in a car crash just outside town on the Barandas road. Since then, travellers swear she still appears - a polite hitchhiker in white who vanishes mid-ride.
The Uniondale Ghost has become one of South Africa’s longest-running urban legends, blending tragedy, tourism, and a touch of the supernatural.
But there’s more to this “ghost story” than just bumps in the night. Uniondale’s spooky claim to fame has become the town’s most reliable breadwinner. Cafés, padstals, and guesthouses lean into the legend - from “The Hungry Ghost Café” to souvenir T-shirts that proudly proclaim “I Got Ghosted on Route 62.”

This Carte Blanche feature explores how one tragic accident became the cornerstone of an unlikely local economy. We revisit the ghost’s origin story - the crash, the sightings, and the people who claim to have met her - but also the living townsfolk who’ve turned folklore into survival.


Further information:
The piece balances local humour with haunting beauty - part travelogue, part investigation, and part love letter to the Karoo’s weird resilience. It’s not just about a ghost; it’s about how myth sustains memory, and how one small town found a way to make being haunted… profitable.

Press Release:


Small Town: Uniondale

It looks like any other sleepy farming town. But Uniondale, deep in the Little Karoo, straddles the fragile line between myth and memory. It’s a folk tale rooted in tragedy: the death of a young woman. But the Uniondale Ghost has become the town’s most reliable
breadwinner. While cafés, padstals, and guesthouses lean into the legend, some residents complain that the ghost should be left to rest in peace. Carte Blanche takes a trip to ask: How has one small town found a way to make haunting… profitable?

Producer: Latashia Naidoo | Presenter: Masa Kekana

Script:


UNIONDALE GHOST TOWN - FINAL

MASA: “Easter weekend, 1968. On a cold rainy night a young couple were driving along a now infamous stretch of road just outside Uniondale, in the Western Cape. The car crashed and Maria Roux died, while her fiance survived…”
MASA: “Years later, a story emerged of a female hitchhiker dressed in white, who would vanish moments after being offered a lift.”
MASA LINK: “It’s just after midnight on the N9 outside Uniondale, and we’re here to follow the legend of the ghost of Maria Roux. This is where it all began - a crash, a name, and a ghost that still keeps the town famous.”

CELL PHONE FOOTAGE:
LATASHIA: ‘What are you doing?’
MASA: “Let’s go! Let’s go!”


ANTHEA DU TOIT: “Eight years after she passed away, a guy was driving down the road where the accident happened, he saw this hitchhiker next to the road and he stopped, and she got in at the back of the car. And then he was driving all along, and all of a sudden he thought ‘I never ask her where she’s actually going’. And when he turned around, she was gone!”

MASA: “Anthea du Toit owns The Hungry Ghost - a restaurant built on the story that keeps the town, Uniondale, on the map.”

ANTHEA DU TOIT: “Anton Goosen was also doing this song, uhm, ‘Die Spook van Uniondale’ - so he started with a song, and then it just blow up.”

MASA: “The song took the legend national. Every Easter, travellers still make the trip.”

ANTHEA DU TOIT: “We do lots of things. You know, it’s like we have a ghost run with motorcycles, and all sorts of things.”

MASA: “I am sporting some ghost earrings from The Hungry Ghost, from yourself. How has that helped with job creation and just putting Uniondale on the map?’
ANTHEA DU TOIT: ‘It help a lot, the main road actually go past Uniondale, on the outside. So people will specially drive into Uniondale to come and ask about the ghost.”

MASA: ‘Have you seen the ghost?’
ANTHEA DU TOIT: “No, I haven’t.”
MASA: ‘Are you hoping to see the ghost?’
ANTHEA DU TOIT: “You know what, after her fiance passed away, the Maria ghost if I can put it like that - never appeared again. So, ya, I think she’s to rest now, ya.”

MASA: “Uniondale is a Klein Karoo dorpie of about 7000 people, and no traffic lights.”
MASA: “Dirkie Coetzee and his faithful tuktuk Toekie will give us a taste of Uniondale by day…”

DIRKIE COETZEE: “Hi Masa.”
MASA: “Hi Dirkie, how are you?”
DIRKIE COETZEE: “I’m fine and you?”
MASA: “Good, good.”
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Welcome to Uniondale.”
MASA: “Thank you!”
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Here’s some little milk tarts for you.”
MASA: “Ah, you’re a star. These are my favourites.”
DIRKIE COETZEE: “You’re welcome.”
MASA: ‘Let’s take a ride.’
MASA: ‘I’m looking forward to this.”

MASA LINK: “They say you haven’t really seen Uniondale until you’ve done it by tuktuk. It’s not fast - but in this town, the stories make up the speed.”

MASA: ‘This is our stop.’
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Ya, let’s have a look at the water mill.”
MASA: ‘It looks old.’

DIRKIE COETZEE: “This water mill was built about 1850, and it was in use for about a hundred years.”

MASA: “Would it be fair for me to say that Uniondale took a ghost and turned it into a whole tourism economy?”
DIRKIE COETZEE: “There are two sides of this story. Many of them will tell you that we can let her rest. And other people say no, it’s the ghost then we can bring in more people by advertising her. That’ll be good for the town.’ ”

MASA: ‘The ghost put Uniondale on the map. Have you ever had any ghost passengers?”
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Not yet - but who knows!”

MASA: “For most Uniondale residents, what the town offers is far more than a ghost story from half a century ago…”

MASA: ‘Have, have you seen a difference in the rain patterns?’
JIMMY ZONDAGH: “No, there are no differences…”

MASA: “Jimmy Zondagh’s an eleventh-generation farmer and local historian.”
JIMMY ZONDAGH: “So you’ll see there, there’ll be five little flowers on each little bud…”
MASA: ‘Uh uh…’
JIMMY ZONDAGH: “And there’s a bee that’s pollinating it…”
MASA: ‘Your family has been here for centuries. For you, what makes this place so special?”
JIMMY ZONDAGH: “So the first thing is the people around us, fellow farmers, and we all work together very well. And the community’s just a lovely community.”

MASA: “And how did Uniondale come about?”
JIMMY ZONDAGH: “In about 1850 there were two towns - one was called Lyon, and the other one was called Hopedale - and then they amalgamated round about 1850 and then they became Uniondale. Way back, they were subsistence farmers - sheep and cattle and things like that - and then in the later years the guys started farming with goats - Angora goats - and ostriches as well. And in1901 the Bollies brought apples to Longkloof, and then it became a fruit-producing area.”
MASA: “But don’t be fooled by Uniondale’s small town exterior.”
MASA: ‘It’s a tourism hub as well, in its own way. What, what keeps people coming?’
JIMMY ZONDAGH: “So first of all we’re close to the coast, so it’s just a hour’s drive from Plett, from Knysna, from George to get here. And then we’ve got a lot of 4x4 dirt roads over here. And And it’s short, so it’s like a spider, you can just travel in and out of town and you can stay in town.”
MASA: “Jimmy's love for Uniondale doesn’t stop at its dusty roads. He’s also preserving the engines that once drove its story.”
JIMMY ZONDAGH: “So this is a 1941 Chev. It was one of the last cars built in the war.”
MASA: ‘Wow! Does it still run?’
JIMMY ZONDAGH: “It still runs.”
MASA: ‘Wow. I would love a ride in one of these one day.’
JIMMY ZONDAGH: “Any time.”
MASA: ‘This is like a time machine in here - (LAUGHS) - a good one of course.’
MASA: “Can’t get a ride in the Chev… so the Tuktuk will have to do…”
MASA: “Back in town, Dirkie’s tour continues with a favourite pastime in Uniondale.”
MASA: ‘So I told you I’m a golfer, right?’
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Oh, you’re really a golfer? Okay but then, we can play.”
MASA: ‘You brought me to the right place.’
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Ya, look here what I’ve got here.”
MASA: ‘Ha!’
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Some putters for me and you.”
MASA: ‘Wow! Thank you.
DIRKIE COETZEE: “And a ball.”
MASA: ‘Lots to do in Uniondale.’
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Ya. You like to play competition or what?”
MASA: ‘Ah, just for fun.’
MASA: “Do you want to get some putting done?”
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Ya, why not.”
MASA: “I’m a little rusty, but let’s see what we can do.”
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Oh, beautiful!”
MASA: ‘Ha! Yay!’
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Now I can see you can play golf, hey.”

MASA: “Our tour ends with a view few visitors see - Uniondale beyond the legend.”

MASA: ‘Oh, wow, I think it’s the perfect time of day to come here.’
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Ya, it is, it is a very good time to come here.”
MASA: ‘So this is the famous Uniondale Boer War Forts.”
DIRKIE COETZEE: “Yes.”
MASA: ‘Oh wow! Is this all Uniondale?’
DIRKIE COETZEE: “That’s all Uniondale, ya …”
MASA: ‘It’s so peaceful here.’
MASA: “For all its legend, Uniondale’s future belongs to the people still calling it home.”
DIRKIE COETZEE: “The ghost put us on the map, but there is more than just the ghost in Uniondale, and that’s what I want to show the people.”
FTB.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Uniondale straddles the fragile line between myth and memory, and how communities reinvent themselves to stay alive.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: The Uniondale Ghost has become one of South Africa’s longest-running urban legends, blending tragedy, tourism, and a touch of the supernatural.
metadata.Summary: Tucked deep in the Little Karoo along the legendary Route 62, Uniondale looks like any other sleepy farming town - stone churches, dirt roads, and the smell of fynbos in the air. But beneath its postcard charm lies a tale that refuses to die. In 1968, a young woman named Maria Charlotte Roux was killed in a car crash just outside town on the Barandas road. Since then, travellers swear she still appears - a polite hitchhiker in white who vanishes mid-ride. The Uniondale Ghost has become one of South Africa’s longest-running urban legends, blending tragedy, tourism, and a touch of the supernatural. But there’s more to this “ghost story” than just bumps in the night. Uniondale’s spooky claim to fame has become the town’s most reliable breadwinner. Cafés, padstals, and guesthouses lean into the legend - from “The Hungry Ghost Café” to souvenir T-shirts that proudly proclaim “I Got Ghosted on Route 62.” This Carte Blanche feature explores how one tragic accident became the cornerstone of an unlikely local economy. We revisit the ghost’s origin story - the crash, the sightings, and the people who claim to have met her - but also the living townsfolk who’ve turned folklore into survival.
metadata.Further information: The piece balances local humour with haunting beauty - part travelogue, part investigation, and part love letter to the Karoo’s weird resilience. It’s not just about a ghost; it’s about how myth sustains memory, and how one small town found a way to make being haunted… profitable.
